e.t: Agaba is a proper name, rendered as “Agaba” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus: once in Ezra 2:45 and once in Nehemiah 7:48. Without the surrounding verse text, the available information supports identifying the name itself, but not adding details about the person, group, or setting associated with it.

Adari, also rendered Athari, is a proper name identifying a person or family in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 26:44. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific family or genealogical role cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning is the name itself: Adari or Athari.

This word means “nephew,” specifically a “brother’s son.” It is a noun naming a male family relationship, identifying someone as the son of one’s brother. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs 34 times, all in Song of Songs. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines how that family relationship functions in the sentence.

Ainakim, also rendered “Enakim,” is a proper name used to identify a named biblical entity. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Kings 15:22. Because it is a name rather than a common noun or action word, its basic meaning is identification: it points to the particular person, people, or group designated by that name in the passage. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role there.

This Greek LXX noun means “point” or “edge,” referring to the sharp or extreme part of something. It can describe a literal pointed feature or, depending on the sentence, the furthest or most pressing point of a matter. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Esther, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on what object or situation the surrounding text describes.

Alexandros is a personal name, rendered as “Alexandros” or “Aleksanthros.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In this Greek LXX corpus, the name occurs 27 times, in 26 verses, all within 1 Maccabees. Because it is a proper name, its meaning in any particular verse depends on which person named Alexandros the surrounding passage identifies. The name appears from 1 Maccabees 1.1 through 11.39.

This Greek LXX noun means “tree limbs,” referring to the parts that extend outward from a tree’s trunk. It identifies physical tree growth rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint: once in Psalms 79:11 and once in Ezekiel 17:6. Those references establish its use in descriptions involving trees, while the central meaning remains the tree’s extending limbs. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the particular tree being described.

This Greek LXX noun means “respite; relief”—a lessening of strain or a pause from pressure. It can describe the relief a person receives, or a period marked by relief. The word occurs 65 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used across descriptions of rest, hardship, worship, and human experience. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

This verb means to “set firmly against,” describing a determined act of opposition or resistance. It presents someone as standing firmly against another person, thing, or course of action. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 15:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, since the verse text is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “behead”: to cut off a person’s head. It describes a direct act of killing rather than a general injury or defeat. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Psalms 151:7. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, but its precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context.

This Greek LXX verb means “stand aloof from” or “depart from.” It describes someone separating from a person, place, group, or position rather than remaining connected to it. As a verb, it expresses the action of withdrawing or turning away. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Nehemiah and 1–2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the person is leaving.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Astheran; Asthiran.” It identifies a person or named figure rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) data, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:6. The available information establishes its naming function and the accepted English forms, but does not provide enough verse text to describe the individual or add details about his identity. Its precise reference is therefore best understood from the surrounding passage.

This is a proper name, rendered “Bathouēl” or “Vathoil,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a personal designation in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs 12 times in the LXX corpus, across 12 verses, beginning in Genesis and appearing also in 1 Chronicles and Joel. Its specific significance in any particular verse must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

This noun means “first fruits,” referring to the earliest portion of a harvest presented or set apart as an offering. It names produce given from the beginning of the harvest rather than the entire crop. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, the word occurs once, in Nehemiah 13:31. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the first portion of gathered produce.

This word is the proper name “Beroia,” also given as “Veria.” It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:4. The available lexical meaning identifies the name itself, while the reference locates its single occurrence. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “thunder,” the loud rumbling sound associated with a storm. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it names an audible natural phenomenon rather than an action or person. It occurs nine times in this LXX corpus, including passages in Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Amos, Esther, and Sirach. The word is rendered “thunder” in the available English renderings, confirming its direct and consistent sense.

This noun means “money bag,” referring to a container used to hold money. It names an ordinary object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within three verses of 2 Chronicles 24, where the repeated wording concerns the handling and collection of money. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the basic meaning remains a bag or container for money.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a judgment or an opinion—a considered view or decision about something. It describes the conclusion someone reaches or the view they hold, rather than an action itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 3:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a judgment or opinion.

This Greek LXX verb means “devour”: to consume food eagerly or completely. It describes an action rather than a person or thing, so it tells what someone does. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 31:16. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains the strong, thorough consumption of food or something being eaten.

This Greek LXX verb means “tear apart”: to split, pull apart, or break something into separated pieces. It describes forceful separation rather than simply moving or loosening something. The word appears eight times across the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Judges, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Hosea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being separated and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the violent or complete breaking apart of something joined together.

This word means “in two” or “asunder,” describing something divided, separated, or apart. It functions as an adverb, so it tells how or where an action occurs rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament translation represented here, it appears once, in Sirach 47:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is separation into two or being apart.

This Greek LXX noun refers to “natural resources”—the useful wealth or supplies provided by the natural world. It is a concrete term for resources that can be possessed, managed, or used, rather than an abstract quality or emotion. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 2:46. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the word functions in that passage, but its basic meaning points to naturally provided resources or assets.

This Greek LXX verb means “turn.” It describes the act of changing direction or causing something to turn, with the surrounding sentence determining the precise action intended. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 2:24. Because the verse text is not included here, its exact force in that sentence cannot be stated more narrowly, but its central meaning remains the action of turning.

This verb means “write out”: to put something into written form. It describes the act of recording or setting words down in writing, rather than merely speaking or remembering them. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 32:1. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the precise reason for the writing must be understood from that context. Its basic sense remains straightforward: to write something out fully or explicitly.

This Greek LXX verb means to “stretch out”: to extend something outward or lengthen it. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, including passages from Exodus, Proverbs, Isaiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being extended and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains active outward extension.

This noun refers to a “rooter-out” or “destroyer”—someone or something that tears out what has been established and brings it to ruin. Its central idea is forceful removal or destruction, not merely ordinary change or loss. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 3:5. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether the word points to a person, an agent, or destruction described in more figurative terms.

This Greek LXX verb means “diminish”: to become or make smaller, fewer, or less. It describes reduction rather than increase, and its exact force in a sentence depends on what is being reduced. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, including Genesis, Leviticus, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains the same across these occurrences: something is lessened in amount, extent, or degree.

Elika is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 2 Samuel 23:25. The name itself identifies the person, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that individual’s role or significance. No broader lexical sense is established for this name.

This word is the proper name “Elul,” also represented as “Eloul.” It functions as a name rather than as an ordinary descriptive word, so English translations retain it in that form. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Nehemiah 6:15 and once in 1 Maccabees 14:27. The supplied lexical information identifies no broader meaning beyond this name.

This adverb means “continually,” describing an action or condition that persists or is repeated without stopping. It answers the question of how something occurs, emphasizing ongoing practice rather than a single event. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 10 times, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Daniel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the action it modifies.

To revel means to take great pleasure or delight in something. As a verb, it describes actively enjoying or finding deep satisfaction in what is before a person. This word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including Isaiah, Jeremiah, Habakkuk, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the person is enjoying, but its central idea is lively, wholehearted pleasure rather than mere awareness or approval.

This verb means to rise up from something or someone, and it can also describe being raised from death. Its basic idea is movement from a lower or previous position into an upright or renewed state. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 36 times, so it is used for more than one kind of rising. The surrounding sentence determines whether the word refers simply to standing up or to resurrection.

This Greek LXX verb means “ward off”: to hold back, repel, or prevent something from reaching or harming someone. It describes an active effort to resist an opposing threat or difficulty rather than merely endure it. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This word means “sevenfold”. It is an adverb that describes an action or measure occurring seven times or having a sevenfold quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times across three verses, showing a focused numerical meaning rather than a broad range of uses. Its basic sense remains clear wherever it appears: the number seven is being applied to repetition, degree, or measure. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on doing something seven times or on something being sevenfold.

This Greek LXX noun means “breadth” or “width,” referring to how wide something is from one side to the other. It describes a measurable dimension, especially when biblical passages give the size of an object, structure, or area. The word occurs 56 times in the Greek Old Testament, with its earliest recorded occurrence in Exodus 25:23 and its latest in Ezekiel 48:13. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on what is being measured.

This adverb means “courageously,” describing the way someone speaks or acts with bravery and inner strength. It tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or quality by itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees 7:20 and once in 3 Maccabees 7:18. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a courageous manner of acting or responding.

Zambri, also rendered Zamvri, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. It functions as a personal name rather than as a word describing a quality, action, or object. The name appears 17 times in the Greek LXX corpus, beginning in Numbers and continuing through 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance belongs to the individuals named in each passage; the name itself identifies them rather than stating their character or role.

This noun refers to “emotions,” the inward feelings or responses of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, including passages in Exodus and Leviticus and once in Proverbs. Its use in sacrificial instructions shows that the word can name a bodily inner part, while its lexical meaning also points to the emotional life associated with what is within. The surrounding verse determines whether the immediate focus is the physical organ or the feelings represented by it.

This Greek Old Testament noun refers to a waiting maid or handmaid: a female servant who attends or assists in a household. It describes a person rather than an action or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Job, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its basic meaning remains focused on a maid or female household servant, while the surrounding verse determines the particular duties or social setting intended in each passage.

Thoulad, also rendered Thulath, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:29. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity can be stated, but no further meaning or significance should be assigned to the name itself.

This word is a proper name: “Iedoua,” also given as “Iethua.” It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Ezra 2:36. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further, but its basic meaning is the personal name itself.

Iezer is a proper name preserved as “Iezer,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 17:2, identifying a person or family within that passage’s genealogical setting. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or concept in the available material; its specific identity is determined by the surrounding verse and passage. This LXX word should remain distinct as a Greek rendering of the name.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a rider, especially a mounted soldier or member of cavalry. It can describe an individual who rides a horse or, in a collective sense, cavalry forces. The word appears 60 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its central meaning remains consistent across descriptions of military strength and mounted personnel. Its basic sense is the person or fighting force associated with riding, rather than the horse itself.

This word means “corn measure,” referring to a unit used for measuring grain or other produce. It is a noun, so it names the measure itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 6:25. The word’s basic meaning identifies a quantity used in ordinary commerce or food measurement, though the exact amount represented by the measure must be understood from the surrounding passage and historical setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “stalk” or “reed,” referring to a slender plant stem. It can describe a natural reed growing near water or a stalk used as a plant-related object. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, including passages in Exodus, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its basic sense remains the same across these uses: a narrow, upright plant stem or reed. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “gulp down”: to swallow something quickly and eagerly rather than slowly or carefully. It describes an action, not a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Daniel 1:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the rapid swallowing of food or drink.

This verb means “shine upon”: to cast light onto someone or something. It describes light actively falling on its object rather than merely existing nearby. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:19, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated appearances. Its central idea remains clear: illumination directed toward something, with the surrounding verse determining the precise picture. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Greek New Testament term.

This Greek LXX noun means “gilded” and is also rendered “Di-zahab,” functioning as a name or designation. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Deuteronomy 1:1. The wording may identify something called Di-zahab, while “gilded” expresses its associated meaning. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise role in that sentence cannot be explained further, but the lexical sense is limited to these recorded meanings.

This Greek LXX noun means “honeycomb,” the wax structure associated with honey. It names a tangible part of the bees’ work rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines how the image or object functions in context.

Lōdabar is a proper name identifying a place, rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or belief. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 17:27. The name is also represented as Lothavar in the lexical definition. Since the available information identifies the location by name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its specific significance in that passage cannot be explained here.

Mathusala is a personal name, referring to a man named Mathusala in the Greek Old Testament. As a proper name, it identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears eight times across seven verses in the Greek Old Testament, chiefly in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Its meaning here is therefore its identifying use as the name Mathusala; the surrounding verse supplies the details about the person being mentioned.

This word means “testimony”: a spoken or recorded witness that presents what is known or affirmed. It can refer to testimony as a formal witness, a solemn declaration, or a testimony preserved in connection with God’s covenant and commands. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 46 times, appearing especially often in Psalms and also in books such as Exodus and Deuteronomy. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a witness or declaration that bears testimony.

Memphibosthe is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 29 times, all within 2 Samuel, and it identifies the same named person throughout those occurrences. The name is also rendered Memfivosthe in the lexical definition. Since personal names identify people rather than describe qualities, actions, or objects, its meaning for a reader is primarily the person it names; the surrounding verse is needed to understand what is said about him.

This verb means “mingle”: to mix things or people together so that they become joined or intermingled. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, from Genesis through Isaiah, showing a recurring sense of bringing separate things together. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being mingled and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “myriad,” referring to a very great number or multitude. It describes quantity rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 39 times, showing that it is used across many passages for exceptionally large numbers. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being counted, but the central idea remains a multitude of great size.

This verb means “grow numb”: to lose normal feeling or sensitivity. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes becoming numb rather than naming a person, object, or abstract idea. It occurs five times in four verses, all within the Old Testament Greek corpus. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains the diminishing or loss of bodily sensation.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Nebel” or “Nevel.” It identifies a named person or figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in 1 Samuel 1:24, 2 Samuel 16:1, and Hosea 3:2. The name’s precise identity and significance in each passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Nisō, also written Niso, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It appears once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 6:1. The available lexical information identifies the word as a name but does not establish from the name alone whether it refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “pierce”: to pass through or wound something with a sharp point. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times in two verses, appearing in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding wording determines whether the action is understood as physically piercing or as a related use of the same basic action. Its central idea remains making a sharp penetration into something.

This noun means “owner of sheep,” referring to a person whose possession or responsibility is a flock of sheep. It is a specific occupational or descriptive term rather than a general word for any owner. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 3:4. The word’s precise significance in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: someone who owns sheep. This entity belongs to the Greek LXX corpus and should be understood separately from Hebrew and Greek New Testament word entries.

Ozib, also rendered Oziv, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at Joshua 15:55. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. The name itself should therefore be understood simply as Ozib or Oziv, a distinct proper name.

This Greek word means “build”: to construct, raise, or put something together. It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly for building physical things, including structures and cities, and it occurs 405 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books of the LXX. Its central idea remains the act of constructing or establishing something. The surrounding verse determines precisely what is being built, but the word itself expresses building.

οὔτε means “not” or “neither.” It is a conjunction used to deny something or to join negative statements, often carrying the sense that one thing is not true and another is not true either. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 110 times, showing regular use across different kinds of biblical writing. Its precise force in a sentence depends on what negative statements it connects, but its central function remains clear: it excludes or rejects one or more possibilities.

This verb means “sit beside,” describing the act of taking a seat next to someone. It is a straightforward action word rather than a title, emotion, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 2:13. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the physical act of sitting beside another person.

This Greek LXX noun refers to anything joined together into a structure or framework. It describes something formed from connected parts rather than a single separate piece. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, once in Joshua and once in 4 Maccabees. The English rendering “framework” confirms this structural sense in one occurrence, while the broader definition includes anything joined together. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This noun means “multitude; quantity,” referring to a large number or amount. It can describe people, things, or an abundance considered together, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 248 times, so it is a broadly used word for expressing numerical plenty or a substantial amount. Its precise reference—whether to a crowd or to quantity more generally—comes from the immediate context.

This noun means “citizenship”: belonging to a particular city or people with the standing and responsibilities associated with that membership. It can describe a person’s civic identity or the condition of living as a recognized member of a community. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs eight times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2, 3, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is membership in a civic community.

This noun means “purple garment,” referring to clothing made distinctive by its purple color. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 8:26. The word identifies an article of clothing rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is a purple-colored garment or piece of attire.

This adjective describes something connected with sheep, especially a sheep market. Its stated meanings are “sheepish” and “sheep market,” so it functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament wording represented here, it occurs three times, all in Nehemiah. The precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains related to sheep or a place associated with their sale.

This Greek LXX verb means “send before” or “send on.” It describes the act of dispatching someone or something ahead, or sending it forward. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Exodus, Job, Proverbs, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the speaker sends and the surrounding passage.

This noun means “prosecutor’s part”—the portion or presentation belonging to the person bringing an accusation. It refers to the prosecutor’s side in a case, especially the opening or stated position presented against another party. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 18:17. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the word functions in that particular sentence, but its basic meaning points to the prosecutor’s contribution in a dispute.

Reuel is a personal name used in the Greek Old Testament. As a noun functioning as a proper name, it identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 16 times in 15 verses in this LXX corpus, appearing in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise reference belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself is simply the name “Reuel.”

Risōn, also rendered Rhison, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it identifies a person or name-bearing figure, but the available lexical information does not provide a further meaning for the name itself. It occurs three times, all in Genesis 36:21, 36:28, and 36:30. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Rōmemthi-ōd” or “Rhomemthi-oth.” It identifies a named individual or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 25:4 and 25:31. Without the surrounding verse text, the evidence does not establish additional meaning beyond its function as a personal or identifying name.

Sabēba, also rendered “Saviva,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:8. The lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an English gloss beyond these name forms or enough surrounding verse text to explain the individual’s role. Its meaning is therefore the identifying name, while the passage supplies the specific context in which it appears.

Salē, also rendered Sali, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 15:32, identifying a person or place by name. The available rendering gives the name as “Sale,” while the lexical definition also preserves “Sali” as a form of the name. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific referent at that location cannot be explained further.

The word Samos is a proper name used as a designation rather than a descriptive term. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Maccabees 15:23. Because the verse text is not included here, the name’s specific referent must be understood from that passage rather than from the word alone. The word therefore gives the name itself, with no broader abstract meaning established by the available record.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Sēlōnitēs” or “Silonitis.” It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive term, so its precise referent must be recognized from the surrounding passage rather than from the word alone. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs six times, all in six Old Testament verses: four in 1 Kings and two in 2 Chronicles. Its recorded occurrences span 1 Kings 11:29 through 2 Chronicles 10:15.

This LXX Greek verb means “leap”: to spring or jump with a sudden upward movement. It describes physical movement rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs seven times, beginning in Genesis and appearing in several poetic and prophetic books. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea remains an active jump or spring.

The word means “convulsion” or “spasm,” referring to a sudden, involuntary tightening or jerking of the body. It is a noun naming the physical event itself rather than an action someone deliberately performs. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:2. Its central sense is clear and concrete: an abrupt bodily disturbance marked by forceful, uncontrolled movement. The surrounding verse determines the precise way this noun functions there.

This adjective means “solid,” describing something firm and substantial rather than loose or insubstantial. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as a normal descriptive word for material or tangible things. The word occurs 17 times across 16 verses in the LXX corpus, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the noun or object it describes.

gl: tinge the eyelids black with eye paint
d: tinge the eyelids black with eye paint

e.t: This verb means to tinge the eyelids black with eye paint. It describes the act of darkening or decorating the area around the eyes with cosmetic paint. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 9:30, so its meaning is especially specific rather than broad or frequently repeated. The word focuses on the action of applying the eye paint, not simply on the eyes themselves. The surrounding verse supplies the particular significance of that action in its setting.

This noun refers to a companion or partner—someone joined with another in an association or shared undertaking. It describes a person considered alongside someone else, rather than an isolated individual. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times, all in Daniel. The central idea remains relational: a companion is connected to another person through partnership or shared standing. The exact force in any particular verse comes from its surrounding passage.

This LXX word is a proper name, given as “Schedia” or “Skhethia.” It identifies a named person, place, or thing rather than describing an action or quality; the lexical information does not specify which kind of named entity it is. It occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Wisdom. Its exact referent is determined by the verse context.

Sōklag, also rendered Soklag, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX text, both times in 1 Chronicles 12, at verses 1 and 21. Its precise referent in each passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, but the name itself carries no broader lexical definition in the available material.

This verb describes being lowly in mind or humble. It expresses a modest posture rather than self-importance, describing someone who does not elevate himself above others. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at Psalm 130:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is a humble inward attitude. [P03 identity; P03 occurrences]

This Greek LXX noun means “completion” or “sales tax.” It can name something brought to its finished point, while in another setting it identifies a tax or charge. The central idea is completion, but the word also has this specific financial use. It occurs 149 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its precise sense depends on how it functions in each sentence. This LXX word should be understood within the Greek translation corpus, distinct from Greek New Testament usage.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “district governor,” referring to a person who governs a particular region or administrative district. It describes an official with authority over a defined territory, rather than a ruler in general. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages spanning Genesis, 2 Kings, Esther, Isaiah, and Daniel. Its exact responsibilities in any particular passage depend on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a regional governing official.

This verb means to sing a hymn: to express praise by singing a sacred song. It describes the act of hymn-singing rather than the hymn itself, so it focuses on what a person or group does. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 25:6. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of singing a hymn.

This verb means to be suspicious—to regard someone or something with doubt rather than confidence. It describes an attitude of questioning or distrust, not simply noticing something unusual. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in Sirach. The surrounding verse determines what prompted the suspicion and how strongly it is expressed, but the central idea remains doubt or distrust toward a person or matter.

This noun means “brotherly fondness”: warm affection directed toward a brother. It names a quality of feeling rather than an action or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. This limited use keeps the central sense focused on affectionate regard between brothers. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Phoua, also rendered Fua, is a proper name used for a person. It identifies individuals in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs five times in five verses, appearing in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Judges, and 1 Chronicles. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not establish one additional symbolic meaning. The particular person identified by the name must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

Chaslōn, also rendered Khaslon, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a named individual or place in the Greek Old Testament, though the supplied information does not specify which. The name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers 34:21 and Joshua 15:10. Its exact reference is understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “confused mass” or “largeness.” It refers to something viewed as a gathered, mixed, or extensive body rather than as a single distinct item. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in 1 Kings and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense can describe either a mass marked by disorder or something characterized by great size, with the surrounding passage determining which aspect is most prominent.

This Greek Old Testament word refers to smelting or casting—the process of heating metal and forming it into a shaped object. It is a noun describing metalwork rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus 39:4 and 2 Chronicles 4:3. In both places, it is rendered “casting,” fitting its basic sense of forming metal through skilled work.
